# Setup

## Prerequisites

- A **Linux** machine or a SLURM cluster. On a mouse genome, STAR alignment
  measured about 26 GB of memory and the index build about 29 GB; on human,
  about 29 GB and 62.5 GB. A typical laptop is not enough (see [Cluster reference](cluster.qmd)). macOS arm64 is not supported: STAR
  2.7.9a, samtools 1.12 and HTSeq 0.13.5, the versions TTpipe pins, have no
  arm64 builds on bioconda.
- `python3` >= 3.11 and `conda` >= 24.7.1, loaded by your site's
  `profiles/<site>/env.sh`. A one-time Miniforge install in
  `$HOME/miniforge3` works on every cluster; set `TTPIPE_CONDA_ROOT` if it
  lives elsewhere. See [Cluster Reference](cluster.qmd#conda-version).
- Paired-end TT-seq FASTQ files (`.fastq.gz`).
- A genome FASTA and a GTF annotation from the **same source**
  ([below](#reference)), for mouse or another organism
  ([Other genomes](#other-genomes)). A STAR index is built once by the
  pipeline, or you point at an existing one.
- Optional, for GSEA: `.gmt` gene-set files (gene symbols) for your organism.
- Internet access on at least one machine, to build the conda environments
  on first use ([Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.qmd#the-clusters-compute-nodes-have-no-internet-access)).

There is no separate setup script: environments are built by Snakemake the
first time a rule needs them (by default into a `.snakemake/conda` folder
where you launch). The first run therefore takes longer and the launcher job
asks for 16 GB.

## 1. Samplesheet

`samplesheet.txt` is tab-separated, one row per **sample** (one pair of FASTQ
files).

| Column | Contents |
|--------|----------|
| `Name` | Unique sample ID. Used in every file name and matched against count-matrix columns |
| `Condition` | The group the sample belongs to (`DMSO`, `2H`, ...). Replicates share it |
| `Replicate` | Replicate label inside the condition (`rep1`, `rep2`). Used as a batch term in DESeq2 |
| `Read1`, `Read2` | FASTQ file names (needed when `run_processing` is true) |
| `Sequencing_Directory` | Folder that holds both files, joined with the file name (needed when `run_processing` is true) |

```
Name              Condition  Replicate  Read1                         Read2                         Sequencing_Directory
ZFP143_DMSO_rep1  DMSO       rep1       ZFP143_DMSO_rep1_R1.fastq.gz  ZFP143_DMSO_rep1_R2.fastq.gz  /path/to/fastq/
```

TTpipe checks the sheet when it starts and stops with a message if:

- a required column is missing (the header must be tab-separated);
- two rows have the same `Name`;
- `Name`, `Condition` or `Replicate` contains anything other than letters,
  digits, `.`, `_` and `-` (no spaces);
- `condition_order` in the config does not list exactly the sheet's
  conditions, `reference_condition` is not one of them, or an entry of
  `comparisons` names an unknown condition.

::: {.callout-warning}
Each sample is its own row and its own set of outputs. If you sequenced one
library on several lanes, concatenate the FASTQ files per mate first
(`cat lane1_R1.fastq.gz lane2_R1.fastq.gz > sample_R1.fastq.gz`); TTpipe has no
merge step for lanes.
:::

Extra columns are ignored. Because the sample table for DESeq2 is made from
the sheet, `Replicate` is a column DESeq2 sees: give replicates of the same
condition different labels, and use the same label for the same batch
across conditions if there is one.

## 2. Reference {#reference}

The defaults are mouse mm10 / GRCm38 and the GENCODE vM25 annotation. You need
a FASTA (for the STAR index) and the GTF (for the STAR index, HTSeq and the gene
table), **unzipped**.

### The chromosome-name trap

A FASTA and a GTF from different places usually name the chromosomes
differently: Ensembl uses `1`, `2`, `X`; GENCODE and UCSC use `chr1`, `chr2`,
`chrX`. When they do not match, the STAR index cannot use the annotation
(STAR typically stops while building it; this was not tested here), or, if the
index was built with one naming and the GTF has the other, HTSeq finds no genes
and the counts are zero or close to it. The source guide mixes an Ensembl
FASTA with a GENCODE GTF; TTpipe asks you to use one source. At startup it
compares only whether the first sequence of each file has a `chr` prefix and
stops if one has and the other does not; it cannot catch other mismatches.

Matching choices (these URLs were checked to exist):

- GENCODE GRCm38 primary assembly and the vM25 GTF:
  - <https://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/databases/gencode/Gencode_mouse/release_M25/GRCm38.primary_assembly.genome.fa.gz>
  - <https://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/databases/gencode/Gencode_mouse/release_M25/gencode.vM25.annotation.gtf.gz>
- UCSC mm10 chromosomes, concatenated into one FASTA:
  <https://hgdownload.soe.ucsc.edu/goldenPath/mm10/chromosomes/>, with the
  same vM25 GTF (also `chr`-prefixed).

```bash
gunzip GRCm38.primary_assembly.genome.fa.gz gencode.vM25.annotation.gtf.gz
grep '>' GRCm38.primary_assembly.genome.fa | head -3   # chr1, chr2, ...
awk '$3=="gene"' gencode.vM25.annotation.gtf | head -2 # chr1 ...
```

### The STAR index

Either build it once with TTpipe:

```yaml
star_index: '/path/to/mm10_STARgenome'
build_star_index: true
sjdb_overhang: 100        # read length - 1
```

or use an index you already have (`build_star_index: false`). If you build
it, set `build_star_index` back to `false` afterwards. The index must have
been built with a compatible STAR (TTpipe pins 2.7.9a). If `star_index` is
empty and `build_star_index` is true, the index goes to
`<outputDir>/reference/star_index`.

### Gene sets (optional)

GSEA runs only when `gsea_collections` lists `.gmt` files. Download them
yourself, for example the collections from MSigDB for your organism, and make
sure they use gene **symbols**, because TTpipe ranks genes by the `gene_name`
in your GTF. Human symbols against a mouse GTF will match few genes.

## Other genomes {#other-genomes}

TTpipe has no mouse-specific code. A search of the workflows and scripts
finds mouse only in default file paths, comments and the `genome:` key, which
is a free-text label shown in reports. To work on another organism you change
config keys; you do not edit rules or scripts.

::: {.callout-warning}
**What has been run.** Mouse (mm10, GENCODE vM25) has been run on real data
end to end. Human (GRCh38, GENCODE v44) has been run on real data for
**processing only**; DESeq2 and GSEA have not been run on human. Any other
organism is untested. Details in [Validation status](validation.qmd).
:::

### Human

1. Download the GENCODE human **primary assembly** genome FASTA and the GENCODE
   GTF (comprehensive annotation) from the same GENCODE release family, from
   the GENCODE site (<https://www.gencodegenes.org/human/>), and unzip them.
   Both name chromosomes `chr1`, `chr2`, ..., so the names match. Check as in
   [the chromosome-name trap](#the-chromosome-name-trap).
2. Set the reference keys:

    ```yaml
    genome: 'hg38'                     # label only
    genome_fasta: '/path/to/GRCh38.primary_assembly.genome.fa'
    gtf: '/path/to/gencode.v<release>.annotation.gtf'
    star_index: '/path/to/human_STARgenome'
    build_star_index: true             # first run only; then false
    sjdb_overhang: 100                 # read length - 1
    ```

3. `sjdb_overhang` is your read length minus 1 (for 101-base reads, 100). It
   is used only when the index is built.
4. For GSEA, download the human MSigDB collections as gene-symbol files; their
   names end in `.Hs.symbols.gmt` (for example the Hallmark set), and list
   them:

    ```yaml
    gsea_collections:
      Hallmarks: '/path/to/h.all.v<release>.Hs.symbols.gmt'
    ```

5. Raise the STAR index memory in your profile. On the human test
   (GRCh38 with ERCC92, 16 threads) the index build peaked at 62.5 GB, more
   than the 48000 MB that most profiles ship for `star_index` (the `pioneer`
   profile now asks for 72000); alignment peaked at about 29 GB, within the
   shipped 40000.
6. Set `reference_condition` to one of your conditions even for a
   processing-only run; the shipped `'DMSO'` is checked regardless
   ([Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.qmd)).

### Any other organism

You need:

- **A genome STAR can index**: a FASTA of the genome.
- **A GTF** in which every gene has a line of feature type `gene`
  carrying a `gene_id` attribute. TTpipe counts reads per gene with HTSeq and
  builds its gene table from the `gene` lines.
- **FASTA and GTF from the same source**, with identical chromosome names.

Optional but useful:

- A `gene_name` attribute on the `gene` lines. If it is absent, `gene_name`
  falls back to `gene_id`, which is fine for counting and DESeq2 but means
  that GSEA gene sets must be keyed by that id.
- A gene type: `gene_type` (GENCODE style) or `gene_biotype` (Ensembl style).
  It feeds the gene-type filter in the results explorer and the rRNA QC
  metric. The rRNA metric counts genes whose type is exactly `rRNA` or
  `Mt_rRNA`. If the annotation carries no type at all, the rRNA column is
  blank; if it uses other names for ribosomal genes, those genes are not
  recognised and the metric will read near zero, so do not take a low value as
  evidence of clean libraries. Nothing else depends on it.

`htseq_feature` and `htseq_id_attribute` let you name a different feature or
attribute if your GTF is organised differently. Be careful with this: counting
**exons** instead of **genes** changes the science, because in TT-seq most
signal comes from introns of nascent RNA (see [From Reads to
Results](journey.qmd#why-introns-count)). The gene table is always built from
the `gene` lines, whatever `htseq_feature` is.

Gene sets for GSEA must be `.gmt` files whose genes use the same names as the
GTF's `gene_name` (or `gene_id` if there is no name). If no suitable gene sets
exist for your organism, leave `gsea_collections: {}` and GSEA is skipped.

### Memory for larger genomes

STAR needs memory roughly in proportion to the genome (general knowledge).
Mouse measured about 26 GB for alignment and about 29 GB for the index build;
human (with ERCC92) about 29 GB and 62.5 GB. For any other genome, run one sample first, check what the job used with
`seff <jobid>` or `sacct`, and raise `mem_mb` for `star_align` and
`star_index` in your profile ([Cluster reference](cluster.qmd#tuning-resources)).

## 3. Config

Edit `config/TTpipeConfig.yaml`. The shipped file is commented line by line
and [Configuration](configuration.qmd) lists every key. The lines most runs
change:

```yaml
samplesheet: 'samplesheet.txt'
genome_fasta: '/path/to/GRCm38.primary_assembly.genome.fa'
gtf: '/path/to/gencode.vM25.annotation.gtf'
star_index: '/path/to/mm10_STARgenome'
build_star_index: false
strandedness: 'dUTP'
reference_condition: 'DMSO'
```

`strandedness` must match how your library was made: `dUTP` (read 1
antisense, read 2 sense; the guide's assumption) or `forward` (read 1 sense).
If you do not know, run with `dUTP` and look at the QC report's strandedness
panel ([Recipes](recipes.qmd#strandedness-dutp-or-forward)).

Pass a different config with `--configfile`
(`sbatch TTpipe.sh --configfile config/mine.yaml`). Make it a **complete copy** of
the shipped file: the launcher reads `hpcProfile` and `outputDir` from the file
you pass.

## 4. Compute site

Set once per cluster, in `~/.bashrc` (see [Cluster Reference](cluster.qmd)):

```bash
export TTPIPE_PROFILE=profiles/biowulf        # your cluster's profile folder
export TTPIPE_OUTPUT_ROOT=/data/$USER/ttpipe  # where a relative outputDir goes
export TTPIPE_EMAIL=you@university.edu        # optional notifications
```

The profile is chosen by `--profile`, then `$TTPIPE_PROFILE`, then
`hpcProfile` in the config (default `profiles/local`, which runs on the
current machine with no scheduler).

## 5. Dry run, and the tests

```bash
bash TTpipe.sh -n
```

lists every job and runs nothing. Optionally check your Python setup with the
test suite (needs `pytest`, `pandas`, `numpy`, `plotly`, `pyyaml`, and
Snakemake and `Rscript` for the parts that use them; parts whose tool is
missing are skipped):

```bash
python -m pip install pytest pandas numpy plotly tabulate pyyaml
pytest -q tests
```

These tests use synthetic and placeholder files. They check logic and the job
graph, not that STAR, DESeq2 or any other tool works on real data. The real-data
runs (mouse end to end; human processing with the experimental spike-in
module) are recorded in [Validation status](validation.qmd).

## 6. Run

```bash
sbatch TTpipe.sh        # SLURM cluster
bash TTpipe.sh          # one machine (profiles/local)
```

[Running](running.qmd) explains what happens, how to monitor a run and how to
recover from a failure.
